rv.q: LaChanze gets that arc just right in a wonderfully rangy and compelling performance.
Nancy Medina's revival reveals a work that has lost none of its power.
Sixty-four years late and right on time
And Moodie excels as Wiletta, giving us a beautifully drawn portrait of a highly intelligent woman forced to compromise and finally bursting out of the box to tell it how it is.
The only frustrating thing about the show is that it has taken this long.
LaChanze, she is extraordinarily fine, and while it is easy to see why Wiletta is tired of working in musicals, her singing in "Trouble in Mind" is as thrilling as her acting.
An actress LaChanze proves herself to be, and not just when she’s singing, and a hell of a good one at that.
Trouble in Mind does deliver a powerful message.

The work begs to be seen; it's just a shame audiences have to wait until the final moments of Act II to hear the exasperated voice of an actor fed up with a system that has minimized her enormous talent because of her Blackness.
The text still contains astonishing power; it could have been written yesterday.
I just wish this remarkable piece of writing had been given a more truthful production.

Is it to tell us how far we've come or to tell us how far we have to go? The answer that the director gave me was a simple yes. If the same question was asked about the glorious revival, and belated Broadway debut, of Alice Childress's play Trouble in Mind, the answer would definitely be a resounding yes.
It still feels radical to hear what Wiletta states so clearly and passionately about how racism works, not just in theater but as a cultural system.
It is to be regretted that Alice Childress’ Trouble in Mind had to wait this long to reach Broadway but it was worth the wait.
LaChanze is luminous and fierce in the central role, showing us the dignity and warmth that have sustained Wiletta where others might have simply become embittered.
It feels bracingly relevant, even more so than five years ago.
In the end, “Trouble in Mind” delivers a universal truth: Keeping a job too often means giving up your dignity.
Luckily, your life need not revolve around the theater to be hooked by the magnetic performance of LaChanze.
Notwithstanding, 'Trouble in Mind' is worth seeing, as it speaks directly to current concerns in the theater industry
The gravitas, lived experience, and magisterial presence she brings to the role is worth the ticket price alone, and makes a fantastic case for an immediate revival of Gypsy.
Trouble in Mind proves an uneven, problematic work whose history is more powerful than what we see onstage.
The two main reasons to see Trouble in Mind: its path-breaking revelation of still-burning issues rarely addressed so frankly onstage when it was written; its outstanding performance by LaChanze.
This Broadway premiere is long-overdue but oh-so welcome.

cn.t: Childress' 1955 satire about racism in theater finally reaches Broadway 65 years late and proves depressingly relevant, with critics praising its power and LaChanze's performance, though some find the production doesn't fully match the play's sharp bite.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
